title: Designing a payment system

facts.text: When a user clicks the Buy button, a payment event is generated and sent to the payment service, which stores the payment event in the database.

One payment event may contain several payment orders, for example when products from multiple sellers are bought in one checkout; the payment service calls the payment executor for each payment order.
The payment executor stores the payment order in the database and calls an external PSP to finish the credit card payment.
Once the payment has executed successfully, the payment service updates the wallet to record how much money the seller has, and the wallet server stores the updated balance in the database.
Once the wallet is updated, the payment service calls the ledger, and the ledger service appends the new ledger information to the database.
Every night the PSP or banks send settlement files to their clients; each file holds the bank account balance and all the transactions on that account during the day.
Reconciliation compares records in different systems to make sure the amounts match, and may be the most painful process in a payment system.

For a $200 watch paid through PayPal, the e-commerce site records a $200 purchase order, PayPal a $200 transaction, and the ledger a $200 debit for the buyer and a $200 credit for the seller (double-entry bookkeeping).
Reconciliation pain points: records come in different formats, so a layer transforms them into one format; the data volume is massive, so big data processing speeds up comparison.
Near real-time reconciliation uses a streaming platform such as Flink; otherwise end-of-day batch processing such as Hadoop is enough.

A record stamped 23:59:55 internally but 00:00:30 at PayPal falls on different days around a 00:00:00 cut-off; it is marked a temporary break and rerun against the next day's PayPal records, which clears it if it matches.
A reconciliation system is always necessary even with exactly-once semantics, because many places can go wrong; it is a safety net.

notes: thin: the guides give the payment flow and reconciliation only; no requirements, volumes or estimates, data model, API, failure handling when the PSP call fails, or how double payment is avoided.

title: Payment reconciliation

definition.text: The process of comparing records in different systems to make sure the amounts match each other.

facts.text: In double-entry bookkeeping a $200 PayPal purchase appears as a $200 order at the e-commerce site, a $200 PayPal transaction, and in the ledger a $200 debit for the buyer and a $200 credit for the seller.
Records in different systems come in different formats, such as the timestamp "2022/01/01" in one and "Jan 1, 2022" in another; a layer that transforms them into the same format solves it.
Massive data volume is handled with big data processing: a streaming platform such as Flink for near real-time reconciliation, or end-of-day batch processing such as Hadoop.
With a daily cut-off of 00:00:00, a record stamped 23:59:55 internally may be stamped 00:00:30 at PayPal, the next day, so it is missing from today's PayPal records and causes a discrepancy.
Such a break is categorized as a temporary break and run later against the next day's PayPal records; if a match is found the break is cleared and no more action is needed.
Even with exactly-once semantics a reconciliation system is always necessary, because there are many places that can go wrong; it is a safety net.

notes: Concept explained in its own guide; the payment flow is in the Worked example.
